description: Establish grid independence for a CFD result by defining the target quantity, building a systematically refined grid family, sizing the near-wall mesh for the chosen wall treatment, scoring mesh quality, and quantifying discretization error with Richardson extrapolation and the Grid Convergence Index.

steps.description: Fix the scalar quantity of interest the study must converge and the tolerance that defines convergence, so that every later mesh decision is judged against one number rather than a picture.

inputs.name: simulation-objective
inputs.desc: What the CFD study must predict (drag, heat transfer, pressure drop, separation point) and the decision it feeds

inputs.name: geometry-and-flow-conditions
inputs.desc: Reference length, inlet velocity, fluid properties, Reynolds and Mach numbers

outputs.name: target-quantity
outputs.desc: One or two scalar quantities of interest with their definition, for example drag coefficient Cd or area-averaged Nusselt number

outputs.name: convergence-tolerance
outputs.desc: Allowed grid-induced uncertainty on the target quantity, stated as a percent band such as 2 percent of Cd

process: Pick a scalar quantity of interest that maps directly to the engineering decision. Integrated quantities such as drag coefficient Cd = 2*Fx/(rho*U^2*A), lift, total pressure drop, or area-averaged Nusselt number converge faster and more monotonically than point values like peak wall shear, so prefer them when the decision allows.

Compute the reference Reynolds number Re = rho*U*L/mu and Mach number Ma = U/c. These set whether the flow is laminar or turbulent and whether compressibility matters, which in turn drives near-wall resolution and the grid count you must budget for.

State the convergence tolerance as a percent of the target, not as an absolute residual. A typical external-aerodynamics drag study targets grid-induced uncertainty under 2 percent of Cd; a heat-transfer study often needs 5 percent on Nusselt number because wall-gradient quantities are more mesh-sensitive.

Separate iterative convergence from grid convergence. Drive solver residuals down at least 3 to 4 orders of magnitude and confirm the target quantity is steady to within one tenth of the grid tolerance before you trust any single mesh, otherwise an unconverged solve masquerades as mesh error.

Record the operating point (angle of attack, mass flow, wall temperature) that the convergence study locks to. Grid independence is established at one condition; document that the chosen mesh must be re-checked if the flow regime changes, for example when separation appears at higher incidence.

steps.description: Generate at least three systematically refined meshes with a constant refinement ratio so that the discretization error can be fit to a power law rather than guessed from two arbitrary grids.

inputs.name: target-quantity
inputs.desc: The scalar quantity of interest to be tracked across grids

inputs.name: convergence-tolerance
inputs.desc: Allowed grid-induced uncertainty band

outputs.name: grid-family
outputs.desc: Three or more meshes (coarse, medium, fine) with recorded cell counts and representative cell size h for each

outputs.name: refinement-ratio
outputs.desc: The constant ratio r = h_coarse/h_fine applied between successive grids, with r at least 1.3

process: Build three meshes minimum. Two grids can only give a difference, not an order of accuracy; three let you solve for the observed order p and detect whether you are in the asymptotic range. Four grids are better when the observed order is uncertain.

Refine in every direction together by a constant ratio. Define the representative cell size h = (V_domain/N_cells)^(1/3) for 3D (use 1/2 power for 2D). Keep the grid refinement ratio r = h_coarse/h_fine constant between levels, with r >= 1.3 so the change in h is large enough to separate signal from noise.

A uniform global refinement by r = 2 in each direction multiplies cell count by 8 in 3D, so budget memory and run time accordingly. When 8x is unaffordable, use r = 1.5 (about 3.4x cells) but never drop below 1.3.

Preserve topology and relative spacing across the family. The boundary-layer growth rate, the surface-to-volume size transition, and the refinement regions must scale uniformly; if only part of the mesh refines, the observed order p becomes meaningless because different regions converge at different rates.

Run all three meshes at the identical operating point and discretization scheme (same flux limiter, same turbulence model, same wall treatment). Record cell count and h for each. Changing the scheme between grids confounds spatial error with scheme error and invalidates the extrapolation.

steps.description: Size the first cell height off every solid wall to the dimensionless distance y-plus that the chosen turbulence wall treatment requires, because a mesh that violates its wall model gives a confidently wrong answer at any density.

inputs.name: grid-family
inputs.desc: The refined meshes needing near-wall layer sizing

inputs.name: geometry-and-flow-conditions
inputs.desc: Velocity, density, viscosity, and reference length for wall-shear estimation

outputs.name: first-cell-height
outputs.desc: The wall-normal size of the first cell for each wall treatment option, in physical units

outputs.name: wall-treatment-choice
outputs.desc: Whether the mesh resolves the viscous sublayer (y-plus about 1) or uses wall functions (y-plus 30 to 300)

process: Define the wall coordinate y-plus = rho*u_tau*y/mu, where u_tau = sqrt(tau_w/rho) is the friction velocity and y is the distance to the first cell center. The wall treatment dictates the y-plus you must hit, and the first cell height is what you control to get there.

Choose the wall treatment first. Wall-resolved integration to the wall needs y-plus about 1 (first cell inside the viscous sublayer, y-plus < 5, ideally near 1) and is required for accurate separation and heat transfer. Wall functions bridge the near-wall region and need the first cell center in the log layer, 30 <= y-plus <= 300, which saves cells but assumes an attached equilibrium boundary layer.

Estimate wall shear before meshing. For a flat-plate turbulent boundary layer the skin-friction coefficient is Cf = 0.058*Re_x^(-0.2); then tau_w = 0.5*Cf*rho*U^2 and u_tau = sqrt(tau_w/rho). Invert the y-plus definition to get the target first cell height y = y_plus_target*mu/(rho*u_tau).

Worked number: air at U = 30 m/s, L = 1 m, rho = 1.2 kg/m^3, mu = 1.8e-5 Pa*s gives Re_L about 2.0e6, Cf about 0.0037, tau_w about 2.0 Pa, u_tau about 1.3 m/s. For y-plus = 1 the first cell height is roughly 1.2e-5 m (12 microns); for wall functions at y-plus = 50 it is roughly 6e-4 m.

Set the prism-layer stack to carry the boundary layer, not just the first cell. Use a growth rate of 1.1 to 1.2 between layers and enough layers that the prism-to-tet transition sits outside the boundary layer (10 to 20 wall units thick is a start; aim to place 15 or more cells across the boundary-layer thickness).

Verify y-plus from the solution, not the mesh. Compute the actual y-plus field after the first converged run and re-mesh if large patches fall in the buffer layer (5 < y-plus < 30), where neither sublayer resolution nor wall functions are valid and errors are largest.

steps.description: Score the cell-level quality of each mesh against skewness, aspect ratio, orthogonality, and growth-rate limits, because convergence theory assumes well-shaped cells and degenerate elements inject error that no refinement removes.

inputs.name: grid-family
inputs.desc: The meshes to be quality-checked

inputs.name: first-cell-height
inputs.desc: Near-wall sizing that drives local aspect ratio

outputs.name: quality-metrics
outputs.desc: Distributions of skewness, orthogonal quality, aspect ratio, and growth rate with the worst-cell values flagged

outputs.name: mesh-defect-list
outputs.desc: Locations and cell counts failing quality limits, with the remedy for each (local refinement, smoothing, re-blocking)

process: Check equiangle skewness, defined as max((theta_max - theta_e)/(180 - theta_e), (theta_e - theta_min)/theta_e) where theta_e is the ideal cell angle. Keep the maximum below 0.85 for the general field and below 0.9 absolute; a single cell above 0.95 can stall or diverge the solver.

Check orthogonal quality, the alignment between the face normal and the vector joining adjacent cell centers. Values near 1 are ideal; keep the minimum above 0.1, and above 0.15 near walls where gradients are steep. Low orthogonality forces non-orthogonal correction terms that slow convergence and add diffusion.

Check aspect ratio. High aspect ratio (length over width) is acceptable and expected inside the boundary layer, where 100 to 1000 is normal for prism layers aligned with the flow, but high aspect ratio in regions of multidirectional gradients (stagnation, separation) degrades accuracy. Flag cells over aspect ratio 100 that sit outside attached boundary layers.

Check volume growth rate between neighboring cells. Keep the ratio under about 1.2 in smooth regions and under 1.3 anywhere; abrupt size jumps act like a numerical interface that reflects and smears gradients. The prism-layer growth rate from the near-wall step feeds directly into this limit.

Confirm a positive Jacobian (no inverted or negative-volume cells) on every element; even one inverted cell makes the discretization invalid. Build a defect list that maps each failing metric to a fix: local refinement for size jumps, surface smoothing for skew, and re-blocking or boundary-layer capping for the worst skew clusters near sharp features.

steps.description: Compute the observed order of accuracy, the Richardson-extrapolated grid-independent value, and the Grid Convergence Index so the discretization uncertainty is reported as a number with an error bar instead of a claim.

inputs.name: grid-family
inputs.desc: Three or more meshes with recorded cell size h

inputs.name: refinement-ratio
inputs.desc: The constant refinement ratio r between grids

inputs.name: target-quantity
inputs.desc: The scalar quantity of interest evaluated on each grid

inputs.name: convergence-tolerance
inputs.desc: The acceptance band for grid-induced uncertainty

outputs.name: observed-order
outputs.desc: The fitted order of accuracy p from the three grid solutions, compared against the scheme formal order

outputs.name: grid-independent-value
outputs.desc: The Richardson-extrapolated estimate of the quantity at zero cell size, f_exact

outputs.name: grid-convergence-index
outputs.desc: The GCI uncertainty band on the fine-grid result, with a pass or fail against the tolerance

process: Order the three solutions f1 (fine), f2 (medium), f3 (coarse) with constant ratio r. Compute the observed order of accuracy p = ln((f3 - f2)/(f2 - f1)) / ln(r). For a nominally second-order scheme expect p near 2; a p far from the formal order signals you are not in the asymptotic range or that limiters and wall models are degrading accuracy.

Compute the Richardson-extrapolated value f_exact = f1 + (f1 - f2)/(r^p - 1), the estimate of the quantity as cell size goes to zero. This is the best available truth from the family and the anchor for the error band.

Compute the fine-grid Grid Convergence Index GCI_fine = Fs*|(f2 - f1)/f1|/(r^p - 1), using the safety factor Fs = 1.25 when three or more grids are used (use Fs = 3 for only two grids). The GCI is the recommended uncertainty band on the fine-grid solution, expressed as a percent.

Confirm the asymptotic range with the ratio GCI_medium/(r^p*GCI_fine); a value near 1.0 (say 0.9 to 1.1) means the grids lie in the asymptotic range and the extrapolation is trustworthy. If it is far from 1, add a finer grid before reporting.

Compare GCI_fine to the convergence tolerance. If GCI_fine is within the band, declare the fine (or even medium) mesh grid-independent and report the quantity as f_exact plus or minus GCI. If it exceeds the band, refine further or improve near-wall resolution and repeat, rather than accepting the finest mesh by default.

Watch for non-monotonic convergence, where (f3 - f2) and (f2 - f1) have opposite signs. This makes p complex or negative and the GCI formula invalid; it usually means oscillatory grid behavior from an unconverged solve, a y-plus in the buffer layer, or quality defects, each of which must be fixed before the error estimate means anything.

description: Run a defensible linear structural finite element analysis from idealization and element choice through boundary conditions, mesh convergence, singularity treatment, and quantitative validation, so the reported stresses carry a known accuracy rather than a colored contour plot.

steps.description: Reduce the real part to the simplest model dimension and element type that still captures the load path, because element order and shape decide whether the mesh converges from above or locks solid.

inputs.name: part-and-loading
inputs.desc: Geometry, material, and the loads and supports the part sees in service

inputs.name: analysis-goal
inputs.desc: What the analysis must deliver (peak stress, deflection, buckling margin, fatigue life)

outputs.name: model-idealization
outputs.desc: The chosen dimensional reduction (beam, shell, axisymmetric, or solid) with the assumptions it imposes

outputs.name: element-selection
outputs.desc: Element family and interpolation order with the reason, for example quadratic tetrahedra for a cast bracket

process: Choose the lowest model dimension that still carries the load path. Use beam elements when one dimension dominates and sections stay plane; shell elements when thickness is under about one tenth of the in-plane size and bending matters; axisymmetric when geometry and load share an axis; solid elements only when thickness effects, contact, or 3D stress states require them. Each reduction cuts cost by orders of magnitude but imposes kinematic assumptions you must honor.

Match element order to the quantity of interest. Linear elements give constant strain per element and need many to resolve a gradient; quadratic (second-order) elements give linear strain and resolve bending with far fewer. For stress, prefer quadratic.

Avoid linear tetrahedra (the 4-node C3D4) for stress. They are overly stiff and under-predict displacement and stress; they lock in bending and near-incompressible response. Use 10-node quadratic tetrahedra (C3D10) for complex cast or machined geometry, or 8-node hexahedra (C3D8 and its reduced or incompatible-mode variants) for sweepable geometry.

Guard against locking modes. Fully integrated linear hexahedra shear-lock in bending; reduced integration risks hourglass zero-energy modes that need hourglass control; near-incompressible materials (rubber, metals in plastic flow, Poisson ratio near 0.5) need hybrid or reduced-integration formulations. Name the formulation, not just the element shape.

Write the idealization assumptions down as acceptance conditions. For example, a shell model is valid only while through-thickness stress stays small relative to membrane and bending stress; record the check that will confirm the idealization held once results exist, so the model is falsifiable rather than merely plausible.

steps.description: Apply constraints and loads that represent the real support stiffness without over-constraining or leaving rigid-body modes, because boundary conditions set the answer more than the mesh does.

inputs.name: model-idealization
inputs.desc: The dimensional model that the loads and supports attach to

inputs.name: part-and-loading
inputs.desc: Service loads, support interfaces, and symmetry

outputs.name: constraint-set
outputs.desc: The applied supports, symmetry planes, and coupling/connector definitions with their stiffness assumptions

outputs.name: load-set
outputs.desc: The applied loads as pressures, tractions, or distributed forces, with point loads avoided where possible

process: Remove all six rigid-body modes without adding spurious stiffness. In 3D the model needs exactly enough constraint to prevent translation and rotation; under-constraint leaves a singular stiffness matrix and the solver fails or returns garbage, while over-constraint invents support reactions that did not exist and depresses stress.

Represent real support compliance rather than idealized clamps. A bolted flange is not fully fixed; use a bolt-preload connector or a spring representing joint stiffness. A fully fixed face at a stress-critical location creates an artificial stress concentration; move the constraint away from the region of interest or use a softer, more realistic representation.

Use symmetry only when geometry, material, loads, and expected response are all symmetric. Apply symmetry boundary conditions (zero normal displacement, zero in-plane rotation on the cut plane) to cut cost. Never use symmetry for buckling or modal analysis, which have antisymmetric modes that a symmetric model cannot see.

Spread loads as pressures or surface tractions, not point forces. A concentrated force on a solid mesh creates a stress singularity at the node that refines to infinity; distribute it over its true contact patch, or use a coupling or distributing constraint that spreads the load to a set of nodes with a controlled stiffness.

Check the free-body balance before trusting anything. The sum of support reactions must equal the applied load to within solver tolerance (better than 0.1 percent); a mismatch means a load or constraint is wrong. Inspect the deformed shape at a large scale factor to confirm the part moves the way physical intuition expects.

steps.description: Refine the mesh in the region of interest until the quantity of interest stops changing, tracking convergence on stress and on strain energy so the reported value is mesh-independent away from singularities.

inputs.name: element-selection
inputs.desc: Element family and order used for refinement

inputs.name: constraint-set
inputs.desc: Supports held fixed across the refinement study

inputs.name: load-set
inputs.desc: Loads held fixed across the refinement study

outputs.name: converged-mesh
outputs.desc: The mesh at which the quantity of interest changes by less than the acceptance band under further refinement

outputs.name: convergence-record
outputs.desc: The table of quantity of interest versus element size showing the asymptote and the percent change at the accepted mesh

process: Refine locally where gradients are steep (fillets, holes, section changes) and keep the mesh coarse in low-gradient regions. A uniform fine mesh wastes elements; use at least 3 to 4 quadratic elements through a fillet radius to resolve the surface stress gradient.

Run an h-refinement sequence: solve the same model at successively smaller element sizes and plot the quantity of interest (peak von Mises stress or a target deflection) against element size or degrees of freedom. Convergence from above is typical for displacement-based elements because they are too stiff and soften as they refine.

Accept the mesh where the quantity of interest changes by less than about 5 percent between successive refinements, measured away from any singular point. Report the converged value and the percent change at acceptance so the reader sees the remaining discretization error.

Cross-check with a global energy measure. Total strain energy converges smoothly even when a local stress is noisy; a stable strain energy with a still-climbing local stress is the fingerprint of a singularity, not of a real stress the mesh has yet to resolve.

Compute von Mises stress sigma_vm = sqrt(0.5*((s1 - s2)^2 + (s2 - s3)^2 + (s3 - s1)^2)) from the principal stresses for ductile-metal yield assessment, and track that scalar through the refinement rather than a single stress component, which can be mesh-orientation sensitive.

steps.description: Distinguish a true stress concentration from a numerical singularity and handle the singularity with fillet geometry, submodeling, or stress linearization, so refinement is not chasing an infinite value.

inputs.name: converged-mesh
inputs.desc: The mesh whose peak stress is under scrutiny

inputs.name: convergence-record
inputs.desc: The refinement history that reveals a non-converging local stress

outputs.name: singularity-classification
outputs.desc: Whether each hot spot is a real concentration (converges) or a modeling singularity (diverges with refinement)

outputs.name: linearized-or-submodel-stress
outputs.desc: The usable stress at each singular feature from stress linearization or a geometrically corrected submodel

process: Diagnose the singularity by its refinement signature. At a sharp reentrant corner the linear-elastic stress behaves like r^(lambda-1) as the distance r to the corner goes to zero, with lambda < 1, so the peak stress climbs without bound as the mesh shrinks. A stress that rises by roughly a constant percentage at each halving of element size is singular; a stress that flattens to an asymptote is a real concentration.

List the usual singularity sources: sharp reentrant corners (zero fillet radius), point loads and point supports, and corners of bonded or tied interfaces where materials with different stiffness meet. Each is an artifact of the idealization, not a physical infinite stress.

For sharp corners that are physically rounded, add the real fillet radius and re-mesh. The true stress is finite and set by the radius; a fillet of radius equal to a few percent of the local dimension, meshed with 3 or more quadratic elements across the arc, recovers a converging peak stress.

For pressure-vessel and weld assessment where the geometry is genuinely sharp, use stress linearization across the section per the ASME Section VIII Division 2 approach: integrate the through-thickness stress into a membrane component (average) and a bending component (linear), and assess those against category limits instead of the singular peak. The membrane plus bending stress is finite and mesh-independent even when the surface peak is not.

For local detail near a singular feature on a large model, build a submodel: cut a small region, drive its cut boundaries with displacements interpolated from the global solution, and mesh it finely with corrected geometry. This resolves the local field at reasonable cost while keeping the global model coarse, and it forces you to supply the real radius that removes the singularity.

steps.description: Validate the finite element result against an independent calculation and quantify the remaining discretization error, so the analysis is accepted on evidence rather than on the authority of the contour plot.

inputs.name: converged-mesh
inputs.desc: The accepted mesh and its solution

inputs.name: linearized-or-submodel-stress
inputs.desc: The usable stress values from singularity handling

inputs.name: analysis-goal
inputs.desc: The deliverable the validation must support

outputs.name: validation-evidence
outputs.desc: Independent checks (hand calculation, handbook factor, reaction balance, energy check) with the percent agreement for each

outputs.name: error-estimate
outputs.desc: The estimated discretization error on the reported quantity, for example from a recovery-based error estimator

process: Check global equilibrium first. The sum of reaction forces at supports must equal the applied external load to within 0.1 percent in each direction; the reaction moments must balance the applied moments. A failure here invalidates everything downstream and usually points to a boundary condition or load-application error.

Compare against an independent closed-form or handbook estimate in a region where one exists. For a hole in a wide plate under tension the elastic stress concentration factor is about 3.0 (Kt = 3 for a small circular hole); for a notch use a Peterson chart factor. Agreement within 5 to 10 percent in a simple region builds confidence in the model setup before trusting the complex regions.

Use a recovery-based a posteriori error estimator. The Zienkiewicz-Zhu estimator compares the raw element stress field sigma_h to a smoothed recovered field sigma*, and reports a relative error in the energy norm eta = ||sigma* - sigma_h|| / ||sigma*||. Target a global eta under about 5 to 10 percent and inspect the local error map to see where the mesh still needs work.

Sanity-check the deformation and reaction magnitudes against first principles. A cantilever tip deflection should track delta = F*L^3/(3*E*I); if the model deflection is off by a large factor, the element formulation, section properties, or constraints are wrong, not the mesh density.

Report the result as a value with an error band and a statement of what was validated. Record the quantity of interest, its estimated discretization error, the independent checks and their agreement, and the assumptions (linear elastic, small displacement, idealization limits) that bound where the number may be used.

description: Set up a coupled multiphysics simulation by classifying the coupling, choosing partitioned or monolithic solution, transferring data conservatively across non-matching meshes, converging the coupling iteration, and synchronizing time steps, so the coupled answer is stable and conservative rather than merely connected.

steps.description: Identify which physical fields are coupled, how tightly, and over what interface, because the coupling strength decides every later choice from solver type to time step.

inputs.name: physics-and-interfaces
inputs.desc: The physical fields present (fluid, structure, thermal, electromagnetic) and where they interact

inputs.name: coupling-question
inputs.desc: The quantity the coupled model must predict and the accuracy it needs

outputs.name: coupling-map
outputs.desc: The coupled field pairs with the direction and physical mechanism of each coupling

outputs.name: coupling-strength
outputs.desc: A one-way or two-way classification per coupling with an estimate of coupling tightness

process: Name the coupled fields and the mechanism. Common pairs are fluid-structure interaction (pressure and shear load the structure, structural motion changes the flow domain), thermal-stress (temperature field drives thermal expansion and stress), conjugate heat transfer (fluid and solid share a temperature and heat-flux interface), and electro-thermal (Joule heating raises temperature, temperature changes resistivity).

Classify each coupling as one-way or two-way. One-way coupling holds when field A drives field B but B negligibly affects A, for example a temperature field inducing thermal stress in a stiff part that does not change the temperature field. Two-way coupling holds when the feedback is strong enough to change A, for example a flexible wing bending enough to change the aerodynamic loads.

Decide one-way versus two-way with a physical ratio, not a guess. For fluid-structure interaction the structural deflection relative to a characteristic flow length, and the ratio of fluid dynamic pressure to structural stiffness, indicate whether motion feeds back. A deflection under about 1 percent of the reference length usually justifies one-way; larger demands two-way.

Mark whether each coupling is a surface coupling (data exchanged on a shared interface, as in fluid-structure or conjugate heat transfer) or a volume coupling (fields co-located over a region, as in Joule heating or poroelasticity). Surface coupling needs interface mesh mapping; volume coupling needs field interpolation or a shared mesh.

Record the stiffness and density ratios that predict numerical difficulty. A light, stiff structure in a heavy fluid (low structure-to-fluid density ratio) foreshadows the added-mass instability that will constrain the solution strategy, so flag it here before choosing a solver.

steps.description: Choose between solving all fields in one combined system (monolithic) or solving each field with its own solver and iterating (partitioned), trading stability against the ability to reuse mature single-physics solvers.

inputs.name: coupling-map
inputs.desc: The coupled field pairs

inputs.name: coupling-strength
inputs.desc: One-way or two-way and the tightness estimate

outputs.name: solution-strategy
outputs.desc: Monolithic or partitioned, with the coupling scheme (explicit/loose or implicit/strong) named

outputs.name: solver-assignment
outputs.desc: Which solver handles each field and how the coupled system is assembled or exchanged

process: Understand the monolithic option. A monolithic solver assembles all fields into one system and solves the fully coupled Jacobian at each step. It is unconditionally stable for tight coupling and converges quadratically with a Newton method, but it needs a custom solver, large memory for the combined Jacobian, and good preconditioning; it cannot reuse separately validated single-physics codes.

Understand the partitioned option. A partitioned scheme keeps each field in its own solver and exchanges interface data between them. It reuses mature, validated solvers and scales to complex physics, but it can be unstable for tight coupling and needs coupling sub-iterations and relaxation to reach the same answer the monolithic solver gives in one shot.

Split partitioned coupling into loose and strong. A loose (explicit) scheme exchanges data once per time step and marches on; it is cheap and fine for weak coupling. A strong (implicit) scheme sub-iterates the field exchange within each time step until the interface residual converges; it is required for tight coupling and for the added-mass regime.

Pick by coupling strength and density ratio. Use one-way sequential solving for one-way coupling. Use loose partitioned coupling for weak two-way coupling such as a heavy flexible structure in a light gas. Use strong partitioned or monolithic coupling for tight two-way coupling such as a light structure in a dense liquid, where loose schemes diverge no matter how small the time step.

Assign solvers and define the exchange. Name which code owns each field, what is passed at the interface (loads one way, displacements or temperatures the other), and whether the strong coupling is driven by fixed-point iteration with relaxation or by an interface quasi-Newton method, which is the choice the next steps implement.

steps.description: Transfer loads and motions across non-matching meshes at the interface using conservative or consistent interpolation as the quantity demands, so coupling does not silently leak energy or force.

inputs.name: solver-assignment
inputs.desc: Which fields exchange data and in which direction

inputs.name: coupling-map
inputs.desc: The interface where data is transferred

outputs.name: mesh-mapping
outputs.desc: The interpolation operator between the non-matching interface meshes, with its conservation property

outputs.name: transfer-scheme
outputs.desc: Which quantities use conservative transfer and which use consistent transfer, with the reason

process: Accept that the interface meshes rarely match. The fluid surface mesh and the structural surface mesh are generated independently and have different node positions and densities, so data must be interpolated through a mapping operator built once and reused each exchange.

Use conservative interpolation for extensive quantities such as force and heat flow. A conservative map preserves the integral, so the total force transferred to the structure equals the total force the fluid applied; the per-node force is distributed by the mapping weights. This prevents a slow energy or momentum leak across the interface.

Use consistent interpolation for intensive quantities such as displacement, temperature, and velocity. A consistent map reproduces a constant field exactly and is accurate for smooth fields; applied to a force it would not conserve the total, which is why the choice depends on the quantity.

Mind the accuracy on curved and mismatched interfaces. Nearest-neighbor mapping is fast but low order and loses accuracy where the meshes differ; a projection or radial-basis mapping is higher order and handles gaps and overlaps between the two surfaces better, at higher setup cost.

Verify the map before coupling. Transfer a known uniform load and confirm the integrated force is preserved to machine precision for the conservative map; transfer a known linear field and confirm the consistent map reproduces it. A mapping that fails these patch tests will corrupt the coupled solution in ways that look like physics.

steps.description: Drive the partitioned coupling iteration to a converged interface state with relaxation that tames the added-mass instability, so the coupled result at each step is the true fixed point, not a snapshot of a diverging exchange.

inputs.name: transfer-scheme
inputs.desc: How interface quantities are exchanged each sub-iteration

inputs.name: coupling-strength
inputs.desc: The tightness that sets how aggressive the relaxation must be

outputs.name: coupling-residual-criterion
outputs.desc: The interface residual norm and tolerance that define a converged coupling step

outputs.name: relaxation-scheme
outputs.desc: The under-relaxation or quasi-Newton acceleration applied to reach the fixed point

process: Define the interface residual as the change in the exchanged field between successive sub-iterations, for example r_k = d_k_new - d_k_old for interface displacement. Declare the coupling step converged when the relative residual ||r_k||/||d_k|| falls below about 1e-3 to 1e-4, tighter when the time integration is sensitive.

Recognize the added-mass instability. In fluid-structure interaction with an incompressible or dense fluid, the fluid acts as extra mass on the structure, and a plain fixed-point (Gauss-Seidel) exchange diverges when the fluid-to-structure density ratio is large, regardless of time step. This is a property of the partitioned scheme, not a bug.

Apply fixed under-relaxation as the first defense: update the exchanged field as d_new = omega*d_computed + (1 - omega)*d_old with a relaxation factor omega between about 0.1 and 0.8. Small omega stabilizes tight coupling but slows convergence, so it is a floor, not the goal.

Prefer dynamic acceleration for efficiency. Aitken relaxation adapts the factor each sub-iteration as omega_(k+1) = -omega_k*(r_k dot (r_(k+1) - r_k))/||r_(k+1) - r_k||^2, which greatly speeds fixed-point convergence at near-zero cost. Interface quasi-Newton (IQN) methods build an approximate interface Jacobian from the residual history and converge in a handful of sub-iterations even in the added-mass regime.

Cap the sub-iterations and monitor divergence. Set a maximum sub-iteration count per time step (for example 20) and treat non-convergence as a signal to strengthen relaxation, switch to a quasi-Newton accelerator, or reconsider a monolithic solve, rather than reducing the time step, which does not cure the added-mass divergence.

steps.description: Synchronize the time integration of fields that each have their own stability limit, using subcycling and a coupling time step that preserves accuracy and stability across the interface.

inputs.name: solution-strategy
inputs.desc: Whether coupling is loose or strong, which sets how often fields synchronize

inputs.name: coupling-residual-criterion
inputs.desc: The per-step convergence target the time stepping must honor

outputs.name: time-step-plan
outputs.desc: The coupling time step and any per-field subcycling ratios with their stability basis

outputs.name: stability-verification
outputs.desc: The check that confirms the coupled integration is stable and time-accurate

process: Compute each field stability limit separately. An explicit flow solver obeys a CFL condition dt <= C*h/(|u| + c) with Courant number C of order 1, where c is the sound speed for compressible flow; an explicit structural solver obeys dt <= L_min/c_structural set by the smallest element and the material wave speed. These limits can differ by orders of magnitude.

Choose the coupling time step as the interval at which fields exchange data. For a time-accurate coupled transient it is bounded by the physics you must resolve (for example the structural vibration period divided by 20 or more), and it must be no larger than the accuracy of the loosest field allows.

Use subcycling when field limits differ widely. Let the field with the small stable step advance several internal substeps per coupling step while the slower field takes one, and interpolate the interface data across the substeps. This keeps each solver stable without forcing the whole simulation onto the smallest step everywhere.

Keep loose coupling time-lagged honestly. A loose (explicit) scheme exchanges once per coupling step and is first-order in the coupling and can lose stability for tight problems; if accuracy or stability suffers, move to strong coupling with sub-iteration (the previous step) rather than shrinking dt indefinitely.

Verify stability and time accuracy with a refinement check. Halve the coupling time step and confirm the coupled response (interface displacement history, transferred force) changes by less than the target tolerance; a response that keeps changing or grows unbounded indicates the coupling scheme, not the step, needs strengthening.

description: Design a Monte Carlo study that answers a quantitative question with a stated confidence by defining the estimator, sizing the sample, selecting variance-reduction methods, diagnosing convergence, and handling rare events, so the result carries a confidence interval instead of a single random number.

steps.description: Define the random inputs, the output functional, and the specific estimator the study computes, because a Monte Carlo run with an undefined estimator produces numbers without meaning.

inputs.name: system-model
inputs.desc: The deterministic model that maps inputs to the output of interest

inputs.name: uncertain-inputs
inputs.desc: The input variables treated as random, with their distributions and correlations

outputs.name: output-functional
outputs.desc: The scalar the study estimates (a mean, a quantile, a probability of exceedance)

outputs.name: estimator-definition
outputs.desc: The sample estimator formula for that functional and the quantity whose error will be controlled

process: State the random inputs with distributions, not point values. Assign each uncertain input a distribution (normal, lognormal, uniform, Weibull) fit from data or physics, and capture correlations through a correlation matrix or a copula; treating correlated inputs as independent can badly bias tail estimates.

Define the output functional precisely. Decide whether the target is the mean E[f(X)], a quantile such as the 95th percentile, a variance, or a probability of failure P(g(X) <= 0). The estimator, sample size, and variance-reduction choice all depend on which of these it is.

Write the estimator for the chosen functional. For a mean the estimator is the sample average mu_hat = (1/N)*sum f(x_i); for a probability it is the sample fraction p_hat = (1/N)*sum I[g(x_i) <= 0], where I is the indicator function; for a quantile it is the order statistic of the sample.

Separate aleatory from epistemic uncertainty. Aleatory (irreducible, inherent randomness) is what Monte Carlo samples; epistemic (lack of knowledge, for example an uncertain distribution parameter) is often handled by an outer loop or interval, and conflating the two understates or overstates the reported uncertainty.

Confirm the model is deterministic and repeatable given a fixed input vector and seed. Monte Carlo error analysis assumes each sample is an independent draw of the same mapping; hidden internal randomness or non-repeatability breaks the confidence-interval math that justifies the whole study.

steps.description: Size the sample from the target precision using the central limit theorem, so the run is neither too short to trust nor wastefully long.

inputs.name: estimator-definition
inputs.desc: The estimator whose standard error must be bounded

inputs.name: target-precision
inputs.desc: The required confidence level and the allowed error on the estimate

outputs.name: required-sample-size
outputs.desc: The number of samples N that meets the precision target, with the formula and assumptions

outputs.name: precision-model
outputs.desc: The relationship between N and the achieved error, used to plan staged runs

process: Use the plain Monte Carlo error law. The standard error of a mean estimator is SE = sigma/sqrt(N), where sigma is the output standard deviation; the error shrinks as N^(-1/2) independent of the input dimension, which is the defining strength and weakness of the method: dimension-free, but slow.

Build the confidence interval from the central limit theorem. For large N the estimate is approximately normal, so the interval is mu_hat plus or minus z*SE, with z = 1.96 for 95 percent and z = 2.576 for 99 percent. Invert this to size the run: to reach an absolute error E at confidence level z, N = (z*sigma/E)^2.

Size probability estimates with their own formula. For a probability p the estimator variance is p*(1 - p)/N, so the coefficient of variation is CoV = sqrt((1 - p)/(N*p)). To estimate p = 1e-3 with CoV = 0.1 by plain Monte Carlo needs N = (1 - p)/(p*CoV^2), which is about 1e5 samples, and p = 1e-6 needs about 1e8, which is why rare events demand variance reduction.

Estimate sigma before committing. Run a pilot batch of a few thousand samples to estimate the output standard deviation (or the rough p), then size the full run from that estimate; sizing from a guessed sigma can be off by a large factor.

Plan a staged run with a stopping rule rather than a fixed N guess. Add samples in batches and stop when the half-width of the confidence interval drops below the target, which adapts automatically if the true variance differs from the pilot estimate.

steps.description: Cut the number of samples needed by choosing a variance-reduction technique matched to the problem structure, so the same precision is reached at a fraction of the cost.

inputs.name: required-sample-size
inputs.desc: The plain Monte Carlo sample size to be reduced

inputs.name: system-model
inputs.desc: Structure of the model that a variance-reduction method can exploit

outputs.name: variance-reduction-method
outputs.desc: The chosen technique (importance sampling, stratified, antithetic, control variates) with its applicability

outputs.name: reduced-estimator
outputs.desc: The modified estimator and the expected variance-reduction factor

process: Use antithetic variates for smooth, roughly monotone responses. Draw paired samples using u and its mirror 1 - u on each uniform input; the negative correlation between the pair reduces the variance of their average when the output responds monotonically to the inputs, at essentially no extra cost.

Use control variates when a cheap correlated quantity with a known mean exists. Form the estimator Y = f - c*(g - E[g]) where g is the control with known mean E[g]; the variance-minimizing coefficient is c = Cov(f, g)/Var(g), and the resulting variance is reduced by the factor (1 - rho^2) where rho is the correlation between f and g. A control correlated at rho = 0.9 cuts variance about fivefold.

Use stratified sampling to remove between-stratum variance. Partition the input space into strata, sample a fixed count in each, and combine with stratum weights; this guarantees coverage of each region and removes the variance that plain random sampling spends on uneven coverage, helping most when the output varies strongly between strata.

Use importance sampling for rare events and heavy tails. Sample from a biasing distribution q concentrated where the integrand matters and correct with the likelihood ratio: the estimator becomes (1/N)*sum f(x_i)*p(x_i)/q(x_i) with x_i drawn from q. The variance-optimal q is proportional to |f|*p; a well-chosen q can turn an infeasible 1e8-sample rare-event problem into a few thousand samples.

Match method to structure and check the correction. Antithetic and stratified need no model insight; control variates need a correlated cheap surrogate; importance sampling needs knowledge of where the action is and a biasing density with heavier tails than the target, or the likelihood ratio blows up and variance gets worse, not better.

steps.description: Confirm the estimator has converged and report it with a confidence interval, using running statistics and batch means rather than trusting a single final value.

inputs.name: reduced-estimator
inputs.desc: The estimator being monitored as samples accumulate

inputs.name: target-precision
inputs.desc: The confidence-interval half-width that defines acceptance

outputs.name: convergence-report
outputs.desc: The running mean, standard error, and interval half-width versus sample count showing the plateau

outputs.name: reported-estimate
outputs.desc: The final estimate with its confidence interval and the achieved precision

process: Plot the running estimate against sample count. The running mean should settle and the running standard error should fall like 1/sqrt(N); a running mean that is still drifting, or a standard error that is not falling at the expected rate, means the run is not converged or the samples are not independent.

Report the confidence interval, not just the point estimate. Compute the half-width z*SE and present mu_hat plus or minus that half-width at the stated confidence; a Monte Carlo result without an interval is incomplete because a different seed would give a different number.

Use batch means when samples are correlated, as in Markov chain Monte Carlo. Split the run into non-overlapping batches, average within each, and estimate the standard error from the batch averages; this accounts for autocorrelation that would otherwise make the naive standard error far too small.

Track the effective sample size for correlated chains. The effective sample size N_eff = N/(1 + 2*sum of autocorrelations) can be far below the raw count; report N_eff so the interval reflects the real information content, not the number of iterations.

Validate independence of the generator. Confirm the pseudo-random stream has adequate period and low correlation for the sample size; for high-dimensional or very large runs prefer a well-tested generator, since a short-period or correlated stream silently biases the estimate no matter how many samples you draw.

steps.description: Estimate small failure probabilities in the 1e-4 to 1e-6 range where plain Monte Carlo is infeasible, using subset simulation or importance sampling built on the design point.

inputs.name: output-functional
inputs.desc: The rare-event probability to be estimated, P(g(X) <= 0)

inputs.name: variance-reduction-method
inputs.desc: The biasing or decomposition strategy carried in from method selection

outputs.name: rare-event-probability
outputs.desc: The estimated small probability with its coefficient of variation

outputs.name: rare-event-validation
outputs.desc: The check that the biasing or conditioning did not bias the estimate

process: Recognize when plain Monte Carlo fails. Estimating p = 1e-6 to a 10 percent coefficient of variation needs on the order of 1e8 model runs; when each run is a finite element or CFD solve, that is impossible, so a rare-event method is mandatory rather than optional.

Use subset simulation to decompose a rare event into a product of moderate conditional probabilities. Define nested failure regions F_1 superset F_2 superset ... superset F_m = F with intermediate thresholds chosen so each conditional probability P(F_i | F_(i-1)) is about 0.1; then p_f = product of those conditionals, and each factor is estimated with a manageable sample by Markov chain Monte Carlo seeded from the previous level.

Use importance sampling centered on the design point for structural reliability. Find the most probable failure point (the design point) by solving for the point on the limit state g = 0 nearest the origin in standard normal space; center the biasing density there so samples land in the failure region, and correct with the likelihood ratio.

Report the coefficient of variation of the rare estimate, because it can be large even when the method runs. Subset simulation typically achieves a CoV of 0.1 to 0.3 for p around 1e-6 with a few thousand runs per level; a CoV that balloons signals a poorly chosen intermediate-threshold spacing or a multimodal failure region the single design point missed.

Validate against an independent method or a crude bound. Cross-check the subset-simulation probability with a first-order reliability estimate from the design-point distance (p_f approximately Phi(-beta) where beta is the reliability index), and confirm the two agree in order of magnitude; a large disagreement usually means multiple failure modes that one design point cannot represent.

description: Build a trustworthy surrogate for an expensive simulation by laying out a space-filling design of experiments, fitting a response surface or Gaussian process, validating by cross-validation, adding points adaptively where the model is weakest, and certifying accuracy on held-out data.

steps.description: Lay out where to sample the expensive model so the surrogate sees the whole input space, using a space-filling design sized to the dimension and the model class.

inputs.name: input-space
inputs.desc: The design variables with their ranges and any constraints

inputs.name: simulation-budget
inputs.desc: How many expensive runs are affordable for building and testing the surrogate

outputs.name: sampling-plan
outputs.desc: The set of input points to evaluate, with the design type and point count

outputs.name: design-rationale
outputs.desc: Why the chosen design and size fit the dimension and the intended model class

process: Pick a space-filling design for a general nonlinear response. Latin hypercube sampling stratifies each input into N equal-probability bins and places exactly one point per bin per dimension, giving good one-dimensional projection coverage; an optimized Latin hypercube (maximin or minimum-correlation) further spreads points so no large region is left unsampled.

Use a factorial design only for screening or low dimension. A full two-level factorial needs 2^d runs and a three-level needs 3^d, which explodes with dimension; a fractional factorial screens main effects cheaply but cannot fit curvature. These suit identifying which variables matter, not building an accurate response surface in many dimensions.

Size the initial design to the dimension. A common heuristic is about 10 points per input dimension for a Gaussian-process surrogate; a quadratic response surface needs at least (d + 1)*(d + 2)/2 points to determine its coefficients, so a 5-variable quadratic needs 21 at minimum and more for a stable fit.

Reserve part of the budget for testing. Split the affordable runs into an initial build set, an adaptive-infill reserve (the next steps spend it), and an independent test set the surrogate never sees during fitting; a surrogate validated only on its training points reports a falsely low error.

Respect constraints and variable types. Project or reject samples that violate input constraints, and handle categorical or integer variables explicitly rather than treating them as continuous; a design that places points in infeasible regions wastes expensive runs the budget cannot spare.

steps.description: Fit the surrogate from the sampled data, choosing among polynomial response surface, Gaussian-process kriging, and radial basis functions by the smoothness and dimension of the response.

inputs.name: sampling-plan
inputs.desc: The input points whose expensive outputs are now available

inputs.name: simulation-outputs
inputs.desc: The evaluated responses at the sampled points

outputs.name: fitted-surrogate
outputs.desc: The trained surrogate model with its hyperparameters

outputs.name: model-class-choice
outputs.desc: Which surrogate family was used and why it fits the response character

process: Use a low-order polynomial response surface for smooth, mildly curved responses. A quadratic model y_hat = b0 + sum b_i*x_i + sum b_ij*x_i*x_j fit by least squares is cheap, interpretable, and smooth, but it cannot capture multimodal or sharply varying responses and extrapolates poorly.

Use Gaussian-process kriging for a general nonlinear response that also needs an uncertainty estimate. The kriging predictor is y_hat(x) = mu + r(x)^T*R^(-1)*(y - 1*mu), where R is the correlation matrix of training points with entries R_ij = exp(-sum theta_k*(x_i,k - x_j,k)^2) and r(x) is the correlation of x to the training points. It interpolates the data exactly and returns a prediction variance s^2(x) that drives adaptive sampling.

Fit the kriging hyperparameters by maximum likelihood. Estimate the length-scale parameters theta_k and the process variance by maximizing the likelihood of the observed data; small theta_k means the response varies slowly in that direction, large theta_k means it varies fast, so the fitted theta also ranks input sensitivity.

Use radial basis functions for scattered data in moderate dimension. The model y_hat(x) = sum w_i*phi(||x - x_i||) with a multiquadric phi(r) = sqrt(r^2 + c^2) or Gaussian phi(r) = exp(-(r/c)^2) solves a linear system for the weights w_i and handles irregular point layouts well; the shape parameter c trades smoothness against conditioning.

Guard the conditioning of the fit. Kriging and radial basis systems become ill-conditioned when sample points are very close or the correlation length is large; add a small regularization (a nugget term on the diagonal) to stabilize the solve, accepting that it turns exact interpolation into smoothing, which is usually the right trade when the simulation itself has numerical noise.

steps.description: Measure the surrogate accuracy honestly with cross-validation, so the reported error reflects prediction at unseen points rather than memorization of the training data.

inputs.name: fitted-surrogate
inputs.desc: The trained surrogate to be validated

inputs.name: simulation-outputs
inputs.desc: The training responses used for resampling checks

outputs.name: cross-validation-metrics
outputs.desc: Leave-one-out and k-fold error measures (R-squared, RMSE, PRESS) with per-point residuals

outputs.name: weakness-map
outputs.desc: Where in the input space the surrogate predicts poorly, flagged for adaptive sampling

process: Run leave-one-out cross-validation for small designs. Refit the surrogate N times, each time holding out one point, and predict the held-out value; the collected residuals give the predictive error without spending extra expensive runs. For kriging there are shortcut formulas that give leave-one-out residuals from a single fit.

Use k-fold cross-validation for larger designs. Split the data into k folds (k = 5 or 10), train on k - 1 and test on the held-out fold, rotate, and aggregate; this is cheaper than leave-one-out when refitting is costly and gives a stable error estimate.

Report R-squared and root-mean-square error together. The predictive R-squared = 1 - SS_res/SS_tot measures the fraction of variance explained on held-out data (target above about 0.9 for engineering use), while the RMSE gives the error in the output units; R-squared alone can look fine while the RMSE is too large for the decision.

Compute the PRESS statistic (predicted residual sum of squares) as the sum of squared leave-one-out residuals; a PRESS much larger than the training residual sum of squares is the signature of overfitting, where the surrogate hugs the training points but predicts badly between them.

Build a weakness map from the residuals. Record where the largest cross-validation errors occur in the input space; these regions, together with the kriging prediction variance, tell the adaptive-sampling step where new expensive runs will buy the most accuracy.

steps.description: Spend the remaining simulation budget where it helps most by adding points through an infill criterion that balances exploring uncertain regions against refining promising ones.

inputs.name: weakness-map
inputs.desc: Regions of high surrogate error and high prediction variance

inputs.name: simulation-budget
inputs.desc: The remaining affordable expensive runs

outputs.name: infill-points
outputs.desc: The next expensive evaluations chosen by the infill criterion

outputs.name: updated-surrogate
outputs.desc: The surrogate refit after adding the infill points, with its improved error

process: Choose the infill criterion from the goal. For global accuracy, add points where the kriging prediction variance s^2(x) is largest (pure exploration); for locating an optimum, use expected improvement, which balances predicted value against uncertainty; for building a classifier boundary, add points near the predicted limit state.

Use expected improvement when the surrogate serves optimization. EI(x) = (y_min - y_hat(x))*Phi(z) + s(x)*phi(z) with z = (y_min - y_hat(x))/s(x), where y_min is the best observed value and Phi, phi are the standard normal CDF and PDF. The first term rewards predicted improvement, the second rewards uncertainty, so EI naturally explores and exploits.

Add points one or a few at a time and refit. After each infill batch, re-estimate the surrogate hyperparameters and re-run cross-validation; adaptive sampling is a loop, and a point added in a region that turns out smooth may change the fitted length scales and redirect the next point.

Prevent clustering and numerical breakdown. Enforce a minimum distance between new and existing points, because infill criteria can pile points on top of each other as the surrogate becomes certain, which adds ill-conditioning without new information.

Stop on a budget or a convergence rule. Halt when the expensive-run budget is exhausted, when the maximum expected improvement falls below a threshold, or when cross-validation error plateaus; continuing past the plateau spends runs for negligible accuracy gain.

steps.description: Certify the final surrogate on independent test data and state the domain over which its accuracy holds, so downstream users know where the surrogate may be trusted in place of the simulation.

inputs.name: updated-surrogate
inputs.desc: The final surrogate after adaptive refinement

inputs.name: input-space
inputs.desc: The domain over which the surrogate is claimed to be valid

outputs.name: certified-accuracy
outputs.desc: The test-set error and prediction-interval coverage that define the surrogate accuracy

outputs.name: validity-domain
outputs.desc: The region of input space where the surrogate meets its accuracy claim, with extrapolation flagged

process: Evaluate on the held-out test set that was never used in fitting or infill. Report the test RMSE and R-squared; because these points are independent, they give the honest accuracy a cross-validation can only approximate, and they are the number a downstream user should rely on.

Check prediction-interval coverage for probabilistic surrogates. For a kriging model, confirm that about 95 percent of test points fall within the predicted 95 percent interval y_hat plus or minus 1.96*s; under-coverage means the model understates its own uncertainty and will mislead any reliability or optimization study that trusts the variance.

State the validity domain explicitly. The surrogate is accurate inside the convex hull (or box) of the training points and degrades outside it; mark extrapolation regions as out of scope, because kriging reverts to the trend mean and polynomials diverge beyond the data, often silently.

Report accuracy per output and per region if it varies. A single global error can hide a region where the surrogate is poor; if the weakness map showed a hard subregion, report its local error separately so users do not apply a 2 percent global claim in a 20 percent local pocket.

Hand off the surrogate with its provenance. Record the design type and size, the model class and hyperparameters, the cross-validation and test errors, and the validity domain, so the surrogate can be used, audited, and retired when the underlying simulation or input ranges change.

description: Formulate and solve a design optimization that accounts for uncertain inputs by characterizing the uncertainty, choosing a stochastic formulation, reforming chance constraints into a solvable form, tracing the multi-objective trade-off front, and verifying the optimum by independent reliability analysis.

steps.description: Characterize the uncertain inputs and separate what is random from what is merely unknown, because the formulation and the solver depend on which kind of uncertainty dominates.

inputs.name: design-problem
inputs.desc: The design variables, performance model, and the constraints the design must meet

inputs.name: data-and-knowledge
inputs.desc: Measurements, expert judgment, and physics that inform the input uncertainty

outputs.name: uncertainty-model
outputs.desc: Distributions or intervals for each uncertain input with correlations

outputs.name: uncertainty-type-split
outputs.desc: Which uncertainties are aleatory (random) and which are epistemic (reducible lack of knowledge)

process: Separate aleatory from epistemic uncertainty. Aleatory uncertainty is the inherent randomness of an input (manufacturing scatter, load variability) and is represented by a distribution; epistemic uncertainty is lack of knowledge (an uncertain model parameter, a distribution whose parameters are themselves uncertain) and is often represented by an interval or a distribution over distributions. The split changes whether you take an expectation or a worst case.

Fit distributions to the aleatory inputs. Use lognormal for positive multiplicative quantities, normal for additive errors, Weibull or extreme-value distributions for strength and peak loads; fit from data where it exists and from physics or standards where it does not, and record the sample size behind each fit.

Capture correlation between inputs. Estimate a correlation matrix or fit a copula; correlated loads and strengths change tail probabilities substantially, and assuming independence can make a design look far safer or riskier than it is.

Quantify epistemic uncertainty honestly as a range, not a false distribution. When a parameter is simply poorly known, carry it as an interval and plan a worst-case treatment, or place a distribution on it and plan a nested loop; do not disguise ignorance as a tight Gaussian that understates the true uncertainty.

Rank inputs by their contribution to output variance with a quick sensitivity screen. A variance-based sensitivity index or a simple one-at-a-time screen identifies the few inputs that drive the output, so the formulation and sampling effort concentrate there rather than spreading thin over inputs that barely matter.

steps.description: Choose how uncertainty enters the objective and constraints, trading expected performance against variability and against protection from distributional error.

inputs.name: uncertainty-model
inputs.desc: The input distributions and intervals

inputs.name: uncertainty-type-split
inputs.desc: The aleatory and epistemic classification that steers the formulation

outputs.name: stochastic-formulation
outputs.desc: The objective and constraint form (expected value, mean-variance, chance-constrained, worst-case over an ambiguity set)

outputs.name: risk-preference
outputs.desc: The stated risk attitude and the parameters that encode it (variance weight, confidence level, ambiguity radius)

process: Use an expected-value objective when many independent realizations average out. Minimize E[f(x, xi)] over design x and random xi when the design will see the long-run average, for example a cost averaged over many production units; this is the simplest formulation and the baseline the others improve on.

Use a mean-variance objective when variability itself is a cost. Minimize E[f] + k*sqrt(Var[f]) or E[f] + k*Var[f], where the weight k encodes risk aversion; a larger k pushes the design toward lower scatter at the expense of average performance, tracing a performance-versus-consistency trade.

Use chance constraints when a limit must hold with high probability. Replace a hard constraint g(x, xi) <= 0 with P(g(x, xi) <= 0) >= 1 - alpha, where alpha is the allowed violation probability (for example alpha = 0.01 for 99 percent reliability); this admits rare excursions in exchange for a less conservative, feasible design.

Use a worst-case formulation over an ambiguity set when the distribution itself is uncertain. Minimize the worst-case expectation max over P in an ambiguity set of E_P[f], where the set is defined by moment bounds or a distance (for example a Wasserstein ball of radius epsilon around the empirical distribution). This protects against getting the distribution wrong, at the cost of conservatism that grows with the ambiguity radius.

Match the formulation to the risk preference and justify it. State whether the owner of the design cares about average cost, consistency, a reliability target, or protection from modeling error, and choose the formulation that encodes that preference; a mismatch produces a mathematically optimal design that solves the wrong problem.

steps.description: Turn probabilistic constraints into a form a solver can handle, analytically where the distribution allows and by sample approximation otherwise, so the stochastic problem becomes a deterministic surrogate.

inputs.name: stochastic-formulation
inputs.desc: The chance-constrained problem to be reformed

inputs.name: uncertainty-model
inputs.desc: The distributions needed to evaluate the probabilities

outputs.name: deterministic-reformulation
outputs.desc: The analytic or sample-based deterministic constraints that stand in for the chance constraints

outputs.name: reformulation-assumptions
outputs.desc: The distribution and independence assumptions each reformulation relies on

process: Reform a Gaussian linear chance constraint analytically. If g(x, xi) is linear in xi and xi is normal, then P(g <= 0) >= 1 - alpha becomes the deterministic constraint mu_g(x) + Phi^(-1)(1 - alpha)*sigma_g(x) <= 0, where mu_g and sigma_g are the mean and standard deviation of g and Phi^(-1) is the standard normal quantile (Phi^(-1)(0.99) = 2.326). This is exact and cheap when its assumptions hold.

Use the first-order reliability method for nonlinear limit states. Transform to standard normal space, find the most probable point on g = 0 nearest the origin, and relate the reliability index beta (that distance) to the probability via p_f approximately Phi(-beta); the chance constraint P(g <= 0) >= 1 - alpha becomes beta(x) >= Phi^(-1)(1 - alpha). Add the second-order correction when the limit state is strongly curved.

Use the sample average approximation when distributions are non-Gaussian or constraints are complex. Draw N scenarios and replace the probability with a sample fraction, enforcing g(x, xi_i) <= 0 for a required number of scenarios; the scenario count sets both accuracy and problem size, so size N from the target alpha as in a Monte Carlo study.

Apply a scenario or sample-discarding bound for a guarantee. Scenario-optimization theory gives the number of scenarios that guarantees the chance constraint holds with high confidence; this converts the probabilistic statement into a finite set of hard constraints with a provable reliability level, at the price of more scenarios.

Record which reformulation is used where and its assumptions. The analytic form assumes near-Gaussian linear behavior, the reliability method assumes a single dominant failure point, and the sample form assumes enough scenarios; a downstream reader must know which approximation produced the feasible set to judge how much the optimum can be trusted.

steps.description: When performance and risk pull in different directions, compute the trade-off front of non-dominated designs so the decision maker sees the exchange rate between objectives rather than one arbitrary weighting.

inputs.name: deterministic-reformulation
inputs.desc: The solvable constraints the search must honor

inputs.name: risk-preference
inputs.desc: The competing objectives, for example expected performance versus variability

outputs.name: pareto-front
outputs.desc: The set of non-dominated designs trading the competing objectives, with a front-quality measure

outputs.name: tradeoff-insight
outputs.desc: The exchange rate between objectives and the knee region where improvement in one costs the most in the other

process: Define Pareto dominance. A design dominates another if it is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in at least one; the Pareto front is the set of non-dominated designs, and every point on it is a legitimate optimum for some preference. Reporting the front, not a single point, keeps the risk trade-off explicit.

Generate the front by the epsilon-constraint method for a few objectives. Minimize the primary objective f1 subject to the others held below moving bounds, f2 <= epsilon, and sweep epsilon across its range; each solve yields one Pareto point, and the sweep traces the front without the blind spots a weighted sum has on non-convex fronts.

Use a weighted-sum scalarization only when the front is known to be convex. Minimizing w1*f1 + w2*f2 over a grid of weights is simple but cannot reach points on a concave part of the front no matter the weights, so it can miss attractive trade-off designs; prefer epsilon-constraint or an evolutionary method when convexity is not assured.

Use a multi-objective evolutionary method for many objectives or black-box models. A non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA-II) evolves a population toward the front and spreads it with a crowding measure, handling non-convex, disconnected, and noisy fronts that gradient methods struggle with, at the cost of many model evaluations (pair it with a surrogate when the model is expensive).

Measure front quality and find the knee. Use the hypervolume indicator (the volume of objective space dominated by the front relative to a reference point) to compare fronts and to check convergence; locate the knee, where the exchange rate turns sharply, because designs near the knee usually give the best balance and are the natural candidates to present to the decision maker.

steps.description: Verify the chosen optimum with an independent reliability and sensitivity check, because an optimum found on an approximated stochastic problem can be fragile to the approximations that produced it.

inputs.name: pareto-front
inputs.desc: The candidate optimal designs to be verified

inputs.name: uncertainty-model
inputs.desc: The distributions used for independent reliability estimation

outputs.name: verified-reliability
outputs.desc: The true constraint-satisfaction probability of the selected design from an independent estimate

outputs.name: solution-sensitivity
outputs.desc: How the optimum shifts under perturbations to the distributions and the ambiguity radius

process: Re-estimate the reliability of the selected design with an independent method. If the constraints were reformed analytically or by a reliability index, confirm the achieved probability with a Monte Carlo or subset-simulation run; a design sized for 99 percent reliability that verifies at 95 percent means the reformulation assumptions did not hold.

Test sensitivity to the distribution parameters. Perturb the means, standard deviations, and correlations within their epistemic ranges and re-solve or re-evaluate; an optimum that moves a lot or loses feasibility under small distribution changes is fragile and should be reported as such, possibly pushing toward the worst-case formulation.

Check the active chance constraints. Identify which probabilistic constraints are binding at the optimum; those are where the design is most exposed, and small errors in their distributions or in the reformulation have the largest effect on realized reliability.

Vary the ambiguity radius for worst-case formulations. Trace how the optimal objective and design change as the Wasserstein or moment-set radius grows; the rate of degradation shows the price of distributional protection and whether the chosen radius is defensible given the data behind the distribution.

Report the verified design with its reliability, its binding constraints, and its sensitivity. Present the optimum as a design that achieves a stated probability of meeting each constraint, with the evidence from the independent check and the conditions under which that claim could break, so the decision rests on verification rather than on the optimizer having stopped.

description: Build a reduced-order model of a high-dimensional simulation by collecting snapshots and extracting a low-dimensional basis, projecting the governing equations onto it, stabilizing the reduced dynamics, bounding the error, and validating the offline-online cost split, so a model that ran in hours runs in seconds with known accuracy.

steps.description: Collect representative solution snapshots and extract a low-dimensional basis by proper orthogonal decomposition, choosing the basis size from the captured energy.

inputs.name: full-order-model
inputs.desc: The high-fidelity simulation whose behavior the reduced model must reproduce

inputs.name: parameter-and-time-range
inputs.desc: The parameter values and time span over which the reduced model must be valid

outputs.name: snapshot-set
outputs.desc: The matrix of full-order solution snapshots sampled across time and parameters

outputs.name: pod-basis
outputs.desc: The reduced basis of dominant modes with the truncation rank chosen from captured energy

process: Sample snapshots that span the behavior you need to reproduce. Run the full-order model at a spread of parameter values and save the state at many time points; the reduced model can only represent dynamics present in the snapshots, so cover the parameter and time range the application will exercise, including transients and any regime changes.

Assemble the snapshot matrix X with each column a state vector of dimension n (the full-order size) and m columns (the snapshots). Subtract a reference state (the mean or a steady solution) so the decomposition captures fluctuations rather than the offset.

Compute the proper orthogonal decomposition by the singular value decomposition X = U*Sigma*V^T. The left singular vectors in U are the orthonormal spatial modes ordered by energy, and the singular values in Sigma give each mode energy as sigma_i^2; this is the optimal linear basis in the sense that no other rank-k basis captures more energy.

Choose the truncation rank k from the captured-energy criterion. Keep the smallest k such that the cumulative energy sum of sigma_i^2 for i up to k divided by the total sum of sigma_i^2 exceeds a threshold, commonly 0.99 or 0.9999 depending on required fidelity; a sharp drop in the singular-value spectrum indicates a low intrinsic dimension and a small k will suffice.

Use the method of snapshots when the state dimension is huge. When n is far larger than m, form the small m by m correlation matrix X^T*X and solve its eigenproblem instead of decomposing the tall X directly; the reduced basis follows from the eigenvectors at a fraction of the cost.

steps.description: Project the governing equations onto the reduced basis to obtain a small system of equations for the mode amplitudes, precomputing the reduced operators offline.

inputs.name: pod-basis
inputs.desc: The reduced basis onto which the equations are projected

inputs.name: full-order-model
inputs.desc: The governing operators of the high-fidelity model

outputs.name: reduced-operators
outputs.desc: The precomputed small matrices and tensors of the projected system

outputs.name: reduced-system
outputs.desc: The low-dimensional system of equations for the modal amplitudes

process: Represent the state in the reduced basis as u approximately equal to Phi*a, where Phi holds the k retained modes and a is the vector of k modal amplitudes. The reduced model solves for a, which has dimension k on the order of tens, instead of u, which has dimension n on the order of millions.

Project the governing equation by Galerkin. For a semi-discrete system du/dt = A*u + f, substitute u = Phi*a and require the residual to be orthogonal to the basis, left-multiplying by Phi^T: da/dt = (Phi^T*A*Phi)*a + Phi^T*f. The reduced operator Phi^T*A*Phi is a small k by k matrix.

Precompute every basis-dependent operator offline. The reduced matrices Phi^T*A*Phi and the projected forcing Phi^T*f depend only on the basis and the operators, not on the online parameter or time, so compute them once and store them; the online solve then touches only small k-sized objects.

Handle parameter dependence with an affine decomposition. When the operator depends on parameters as A(p) = sum theta_q(p)*A_q, project each A_q once offline to get small reduced blocks, and assemble the reduced operator online as sum theta_q(p)*(Phi^T*A_q*Phi); this keeps the online cost independent of the full dimension n.

Confirm the reduced system reproduces a training case before trusting it. Run the reduced model at a parameter and time already in the snapshot set and compare the reconstructed state Phi*a to the stored full-order solution; a large error here means the basis or the projection is wrong, not that the reduced model is merely extrapolating.

steps.description: Stabilize the reduced dynamics and treat nonlinear terms efficiently, because a Galerkin reduced model can be unstable even when the full-order model is stable, and nonlinearities otherwise cost the full dimension to evaluate.

inputs.name: reduced-system
inputs.desc: The projected dynamics that may need stabilization

inputs.name: snapshot-set
inputs.desc: The data used to build nonlinear-term interpolation

outputs.name: stabilized-reduced-model
outputs.desc: The reduced model with stabilization or closure added so it stays bounded

outputs.name: nonlinear-treatment
outputs.desc: The interpolation scheme that evaluates nonlinear terms at reduced cost

process: Expect and diagnose reduced-model instability. Truncating the low-energy modes removes the small scales that drain energy in the full system, so a Galerkin reduced model of a convection-dominated or turbulent flow can grow unbounded even though the full model is stable; check the eigenvalues of the reduced operator and watch for energy growth in a test run.

Add a closure or stabilization to replace the missing dissipation. Options include adding an eddy-viscosity-like dissipation term tuned so the reduced energy balance matches the full model, Petrov-Galerkin projection with a test basis chosen for stability (least-squares Petrov-Galerkin), or retaining a few extra modes purely for stabilization.

Treat nonlinear terms with hyper-reduction, because a naive nonlinear term costs the full dimension n to evaluate even in a reduced model. The discrete empirical interpolation method selects a small set of m interpolation indices and reconstructs the nonlinear term from the values at only those entries, making the online cost scale with m and k rather than n.

Build the interpolation basis from nonlinear snapshots.
