Collect snapshots of the nonlinear term itself, apply a proper orthogonal decomposition to them, and run the interpolation-point selection greedily on the resulting basis; the number of interpolation points m is chosen like the mode count, from the decay of the nonlinear-term singular values.

Verify that stabilization did not destroy accuracy. A stabilization strong enough to bound the model can also over-damp it; confirm on a training case that the stabilized model still reproduces the full-order energy and key outputs, and tune the stabilization to the lightest touch that keeps the model bounded.

steps.description: Attach an a posteriori error estimate to the reduced-model output so its prediction carries a bound, and use that bound to drive a greedy basis construction.

inputs.name: stabilized-reduced-model
inputs.desc: The reduced model whose error must be bounded

inputs.name: full-order-model
inputs.desc: The operators needed to compute the residual and stability constant

outputs.name: error-bound
outputs.desc: The a posteriori bound on the reduced-model error as a function of parameters

outputs.name: greedy-basis-plan
outputs.desc: The next parameter at which to enrich the basis, chosen where the bound is largest

process: Compute the residual of the reduced solution in the full equations. Insert the reconstructed state Phi*a into the full-order governing equation and evaluate the residual r(p); unlike the true error, the residual is computable without a full-order solve, and it is the engine of a posteriori error estimation.

Bound the error by the residual over a stability constant. For many problems the error satisfies ||u - Phi*a|| <= ||r(p)|| / beta_LB(p), where beta_LB is a computable lower bound on the stability (inf-sup or coercivity) constant of the operator; this turns a cheap residual into a certified bound on the output error.

Precompute the residual-norm ingredients offline so the bound is cheap online. The residual norm expands into inner products of basis-projected operator pieces that can be assembled once; the online evaluation of the error bound then costs only k-sized operations, preserving the speed that justifies the reduced model.

Drive a greedy basis construction with the bound. Over a training set of parameters, evaluate the error bound everywhere, run the full-order model only at the single parameter where the bound is largest, add that snapshot to the basis, and repeat; this reduced-basis greedy builds a near-optimal basis with far fewer full-order solves than sampling blindly.

Stop the greedy loop on the bound, not on a guess. Terminate when the maximum error bound over the training set falls below the target tolerance; the bound gives a certified statement that the reduced model meets its accuracy everywhere in the training set, which a snapshot count alone cannot provide.

steps.description: Validate the reduced model on parameters it was not trained on and account honestly for the offline cost, so the claimed speedup is net of the investment and holds where it will be used.

inputs.name: greedy-basis-plan
inputs.desc: The final basis produced by the greedy enrichment

inputs.name: parameter-and-time-range
inputs.desc: The operating envelope over which the reduced model is validated

outputs.name: validated-rom
outputs.desc: The reduced model with out-of-sample accuracy and its validity envelope

outputs.name: cost-benefit-record
outputs.desc: The offline build cost, the online per-query cost, and the net speedup and break-even query count

process: Test at out-of-sample parameters and times. Evaluate the reduced model at parameter and time points deliberately excluded from the snapshot and greedy sets, and compare to full-order solves; in-sample accuracy is expected and proves little, while out-of-sample accuracy is what the application depends on.

Quantify the online speedup against the full dimension. With a reduced dimension k on the order of 10 to 50 and a full dimension n on the order of 1e6 or more, and with nonlinear terms handled by interpolation so no step touches n, the online solve is typically faster by several orders of magnitude; measure it rather than asserting it.

Account for the offline cost and the break-even point. The snapshots, decomposition, operator projection, and greedy enrichment are a large one-time cost; divide it by the per-query saving to get the number of online queries needed to break even, and report whether the intended use (many-query optimization, real-time control, uncertainty propagation) clears that threshold.

Map the validity envelope and its edges. Confirm where in parameter space the out-of-sample error stays within tolerance and mark where it degrades; a reduced model built from snapshots in one regime will not represent a regime change (a new separation, a bifurcation) that the snapshots never saw, and that edge must be stated.

Hand off the reduced model with its certificate. Package the basis, the reduced operators, the interpolation points, the error bound, the out-of-sample accuracy, and the validity envelope, so the model can be deployed in an optimization or control loop with a clear statement of where and how well it stands in for the full simulation.

description: Select the turbulence modeling approach that fits the flow physics and the compute budget by screening the flow regime, choosing a RANS closure or a scale-resolving method, sizing the grid each demands, estimating cost, and validating against the law of the wall and reference data.

steps.description: Screen the flow physics that decide which turbulence approach can succeed, because the dominant features (separation, pressure gradient, transition, unsteadiness) rule methods in or out before any grid is built.

inputs.name: flow-configuration
inputs.desc: The geometry, boundary conditions, and operating point of the flow to be simulated

inputs.name: accuracy-and-output-needs
inputs.desc: What the simulation must predict (forces, heat transfer, noise, mixing) and to what accuracy

outputs.name: flow-regime-profile
outputs.desc: The Reynolds number, expected separation, pressure-gradient character, transition, and unsteadiness of the flow

outputs.name: modeling-requirements
outputs.desc: Which physics the turbulence approach must capture to meet the output needs

process: Compute the Reynolds number and locate the flow on the laminar-transitional-turbulent map. Re = rho*U*L/mu sets the range of scales; pipe flow transitions near Re about 2300, a flat-plate boundary layer near Re_x about 5e5, and high-Re external aerodynamics is fully turbulent with a wide scale separation that forbids resolving all scales.

Identify whether the flow separates and under what pressure gradient. Attached boundary layers with mild gradients are forgiving; adverse pressure gradients and separation (diffusers, airfoils past stall, bluff bodies) are where simple closures fail, because the equilibrium assumptions behind wall functions and the eddy-viscosity closures break down.

Decide whether transition matters. If a laminar run of boundary layer precedes turbulence (low-Re airfoils, turbine blades, small drones), fully turbulent models will mispredict drag and heat transfer; the output may require a transition-sensitive model rather than a fully turbulent one.

Judge whether the quantity of interest needs the unsteady turbulent structures themselves. Mean forces and heat transfer on attached flows are often well predicted by a steady averaged model; aeroacoustic noise, buffeting, combustion mixing, and massively separated wakes need the resolved unsteady eddies that only a scale-resolving method provides.

Translate the physics into modeling requirements. Write down what the approach must capture (near-wall gradients for heat transfer, separation onset for stall, resolved spectra for noise) so the next step chooses a method that meets the requirements rather than defaulting to a familiar one.

steps.description: Choose a RANS closure when the averaged flow suffices, matching the model to wall-bounded versus free-shear behavior and to the presence of separation.

inputs.name: flow-regime-profile
inputs.desc: The regime features that steer the closure choice

inputs.name: modeling-requirements
inputs.desc: The physics the averaged model must capture

outputs.name: rans-closure
outputs.desc: The selected RANS turbulence model with its applicability and limits

outputs.name: wall-treatment-requirement
outputs.desc: Whether the model integrates to the wall (y-plus about 1) or uses wall functions (y-plus 30 to 300)

process: Use the standard k-epsilon model for high-Reynolds, free-shear and fully turbulent core flows. It is stable and cheap and performs well for jets, mixing layers, and flows without strong wall effects, but it is inaccurate in the near-wall region and under adverse pressure gradients, and it normally runs with wall functions (y-plus 30 to 300) rather than integrating to the wall.

Use the k-omega SST model as the default for wall-bounded aerodynamic and separating flows. It blends a k-omega formulation near the wall (integrating to the wall at y-plus about 1) with k-epsilon behavior in the far field, and its shear-stress-transport limiter improves the prediction of separation onset under adverse pressure gradients, which is why it is the common first choice for external aerodynamics and turbomachinery.

Consider a Reynolds-stress model when anisotropy dominates. Flows with strong swirl, rotation, or secondary motions in ducts have anisotropic turbulence that eddy-viscosity models (k-epsilon, k-omega) cannot represent; a Reynolds-stress model solves transport equations for the individual stresses at higher cost and lower stability, justified only when the anisotropy drives the result.

Add a transition model when the screening flagged transition. Couple the turbulence model with a transition formulation (for example a gamma or gamma-Re-theta model) so the laminar run and transition location are predicted rather than assumed fully turbulent from the leading edge.

Accept the shared limitation of all RANS closures. They model the entire turbulence spectrum and assume a separation of scales between the mean and the turbulence, so they predict mean attached flows well but lose accuracy for massively separated, strongly unsteady, or acoustically driven flows, which is the boundary where the next step moves to scale-resolving methods.

steps.description: Choose a scale-resolving approach when averaged models cannot deliver, selecting among large-eddy simulation, detached-eddy hybrids, and direct simulation by what must be resolved and what can be afforded.

inputs.name: modeling-requirements
inputs.desc: The resolved-physics needs that rule out a RANS closure

inputs.name: flow-regime-profile
inputs.desc: The Reynolds number and separation that set resolution and cost

outputs.name: scale-resolving-method
outputs.desc: The chosen method (LES, wall-modeled LES, DES or DDES, or DNS) with its rationale

outputs.name: resolution-expectation
outputs.desc: The fraction of turbulent energy to be resolved and the near-wall treatment the method assumes

process: Use large-eddy simulation to resolve the energy-containing eddies and model only the small subgrid scales. A well-resolved LES captures about 80 percent or more of the turbulent kinetic energy on the grid and models the rest with a subgrid-scale model; it predicts unsteady separation, mixing, and noise that RANS cannot, at far higher cost.

Use direct numerical simulation only at low Reynolds number. DNS resolves every scale down to the Kolmogorov length and needs grid points scaling as Re^(9/4) with time steps scaling similarly, so its cost scales roughly as Re^3; it is a research tool for canonical flows at modest Re and a source of validation data, not a design tool for high-Re hardware.

Use a hybrid RANS-LES method to afford high-Re wall-bounded flows with separation. Detached-eddy simulation runs RANS in the attached boundary layer and switches to LES in separated regions; delayed DES (DDES) adds a shield so the model does not switch prematurely inside the boundary layer, avoiding the grid-induced-separation error that plain DES suffers when the grid is ambiguous.

Use wall-modeled LES when resolving the near-wall streaks is unaffordable. Wall-resolved LES near-wall cost scales roughly as Re^1.8 because the streak size shrinks in wall units; a wall model that supplies the wall stress from the outer flow reduces this toward Re^0.4 scaling, making high-Re LES feasible at the price of modeling the inner layer.

State the resolution expectation the method carries. Record the target resolved-energy fraction, whether the near-wall layer is resolved or modeled, and the subgrid model; these set the grid requirements the next step sizes and are the assumptions the validation must confirm were met.

steps.description: Size the grid and estimate the compute cost the chosen approach demands, so the method is confirmed affordable before a single mesh is generated.

inputs.name: scale-resolving-method
inputs.desc: The method whose grid requirements must be sized (or the RANS wall treatment)

inputs.name: wall-treatment-requirement
inputs.desc: The near-wall y-plus target that sets the first-cell size

outputs.name: grid-sizing
outputs.desc: The near-wall and bulk resolution in wall units with an estimated cell count

outputs.name: cost-estimate
outputs.desc: The estimated core-hours and turnaround, with a pass or fail against the compute budget

process: Size the RANS grid from the wall treatment. For wall-resolved RANS place the first cell at y-plus about 1 with 15 or more cells across the boundary layer; for wall functions place the first cell center at 30 <= y-plus <= 300. The total cell count is dominated by the near-wall clustering and the wake refinement, typically millions of cells for a full configuration.

Size wall-resolved LES in wall units. The near-wall grid needs streamwise spacing delta_x+ about 50 to 150, wall-normal first spacing delta_y+ about 1, and spanwise spacing delta_z+ about 15 to 40 to resolve the near-wall streaks; this fine spacing over the whole wetted area is what makes wall-resolved LES scale as roughly Re^1.8 in cell count.

Size wall-modeled LES and hybrids more coarsely near the wall. With a wall model the first cell can sit in the log layer and the near-wall grid relaxes, cutting the count substantially; for DDES ensure the grid in the separated region is fine enough to resolve the shed eddies and the switch from RANS to LES happens where intended.

Estimate time steps and averaging windows for unsteady methods. A scale-resolving run must use a time step with a cell Courant number near or below 1 in the resolved region and must run long enough to gather converged statistics (many flow-through times), so the cost is cells times time steps times flow-throughs, not just cells.

Compare the estimate to the budget and decide. Convert cell count and time steps into core-hours and wall-clock turnaround for the available machine; if a wall-resolved LES is unaffordable, step back to wall-modeled LES, DDES, or an unsteady RANS before meshing, rather than discovering the infeasibility after building a grid.

steps.description: Validate the turbulence simulation against the law of the wall and reference data, so the modeling choice is confirmed by evidence rather than by the solution having converged.

inputs.name: grid-sizing
inputs.desc: The grid whose near-wall resolution must be confirmed from the solution

inputs.name: resolution-expectation
inputs.desc: The resolved-energy and near-wall assumptions to be checked

outputs.name: wall-profile-check
outputs.desc: The near-wall velocity profile compared to the law of the wall, confirming the wall treatment

outputs.name: validation-evidence
outputs.desc: Skin friction, separation location, or spectra compared to experiment or reference simulation with the agreement

process: Confirm the near-wall velocity follows the law of the wall. Plot the mean velocity in wall units u+ against y+ and check the viscous sublayer u+ = y+ for y+ < 5 and the log law u+ = (1/kappa)*ln(y+) + B with kappa = 0.41 and B = 5.0 to 5.2 for 30 < y+ < 300; a profile off the log law means the wall treatment or near-wall grid is wrong, which corrupts skin friction and heat transfer.

Check the achieved y+ field against the model requirement. Extract y+ from the solution and confirm it matches the wall treatment target (about 1 for wall-resolved, 30 to 300 for wall functions); patches in the buffer layer (5 < y+ < 30) are where both treatments are invalid and should be re-meshed.

For scale-resolving runs, verify the resolved-energy fraction. Estimate the ratio of resolved to modeled turbulent kinetic energy and confirm the resolved fraction meets the target (about 80 percent or more for a credible LES); too much modeled energy means the grid is too coarse and the run is closer to an unsteady RANS than an LES.

Compare an integral quantity to reference data. Match skin-friction coefficient, pressure distribution, separation and reattachment locations, or Nusselt number against experiment or a trusted higher-fidelity simulation; agreement within the accuracy target validates the modeling choice, and a systematic offset points to the closure rather than the mesh.

Compare spectra or unsteady statistics when the output demands them. For noise or mixing, check the resolved velocity spectrum shows the expected inertial-range slope and that the dominant frequencies match measurements; a spectrum that decays too fast at high wavenumber confirms under-resolution and tells you the scale-resolving method did not deliver what it promised.

description: Model a piping and thermal-fluid system as a one-dimensional network by building the node-and-branch topology, characterizing pumps, pipes, valves, and heat exchangers, assembling and solving the conservation equations, extending to transient and two-phase behavior, and validating against energy and pressure-drop balances.

steps.description: Represent the physical system as nodes and branches so a continuous pipe network becomes a solvable set of conservation equations at junctions and flow relations along components.

inputs.name: system-schematic
inputs.desc: The piping and instrumentation layout with components, connections, and operating fluid

inputs.name: operating-conditions
inputs.desc: Source pressures and temperatures, demanded flows, and the environment the system exchanges heat with

outputs.name: network-graph
outputs.desc: The nodes (junctions, boundaries) and branches (components) with connectivity and reference elevations

outputs.name: boundary-set
outputs.desc: The fixed-pressure, fixed-flow, and thermal boundary conditions that close the network

process: Map every junction and reservoir to a node and every flow-carrying component to a branch. A node carries a single pressure and temperature; a branch (pipe, pump, valve, heat exchanger) carries a flow and a pressure change that depends on that flow. This one-dimensional abstraction is valid when the flow is well described by cross-section averages, which holds for most piping systems.

Record elevations at nodes to capture static head. The pressure relation along a branch includes the gravity term rho*g*dz between its end nodes, which matters for tall systems, pump suction head, and natural-circulation loops; omitting elevation silently biases the pressure solution.

Set the boundary conditions that close the problem. Fix pressure at reservoirs and open ends, fix flow at pumps operating on a demanded duty or at metered supplies, and fix temperature or heat input at thermal boundaries; a network with too few boundaries is underdetermined and one with inconsistent boundaries has no solution.

Identify loops and series-parallel structure. Count independent loops for the pressure-flow solve; parallel branches split flow by their resistances and series branches share flow, and recognizing this structure both aids the solver initial guess and catches topology errors such as an isolated node with no path to a boundary.

Choose the modeling fidelity per component. Decide which components are lumped (a single branch resistance) and which need internal nodes (a long pipe discretized for temperature decay, a heat exchanger split into sections); the topology must carry enough internal nodes to resolve the temperature and pressure variation the outputs require.

steps.description: Assign each branch its physical flow relation, pulling friction, pump, valve, and heat-exchanger characteristics from correlations and curves so the network equations have real coefficients.

inputs.name: network-graph
inputs.desc: The branches needing flow and heat characteristics

inputs.name: operating-conditions
inputs.desc: Fluid properties and the operating range over which characteristics are evaluated

outputs.name: component-models
outputs.desc: The pressure-flow and heat-transfer relation for each branch with its parameters

outputs.name: property-evaluation
outputs.desc: The fluid properties (density, viscosity, specific heat) evaluated at the operating states

process: Model pipe friction with the Darcy-Weisbach relation dP = f*(L/D)*(rho*V^2/2), where f is the Darcy friction factor, L and D the length and diameter, and V the mean velocity. Use f = 64/Re for laminar flow (Re < 2300) and solve the Colebrook relation 1/sqrt(f) = -2*log10(eps/(3.7*D) + 2.51/(Re*sqrt(f))) for turbulent flow, where eps is the wall roughness; the Swamee-Jain explicit formula is a good non-iterative approximation.

Model pumps with their head-versus-flow curve and affinity laws. Represent the pump as a branch whose pressure rise follows the manufacturer head curve H(Q); scale between speeds with the affinity laws Q proportional to N, H proportional to N^2, and shaft power proportional to N^3, so a 20 percent speed cut roughly halves the head and cuts power to about half of half.

Model valves and orifices with a flow coefficient. Use Q = Cv*sqrt(dP/SG) for a valve of coefficient Cv and fluid specific gravity SG, or a loss coefficient K giving dP = K*(rho*V^2/2) for fittings; the valve characteristic (linear, equal-percentage) sets how Cv varies with stem position for control studies.

Model heat exchangers with the effectiveness-NTU method. Compute NTU = U*A/C_min where C_min is the smaller of the two stream heat-capacity rates and U*A the overall conductance; for a counterflow exchanger the effectiveness is eps = (1 - exp(-NTU*(1 - Cr)))/(1 - Cr*exp(-NTU*(1 - Cr))) with Cr = C_min/C_max, and the heat duty is Q = eps*C_min*(T_hot_in - T_cold_in).

Evaluate fluid properties at the local state and flag strong variation. Density, viscosity, and specific heat change with temperature and pressure; for liquids viscosity changes most and feeds back into the friction factor through Re, so for systems with large temperature swings evaluate properties per branch rather than once globally.

steps.description: Assemble and solve the coupled mass, momentum, and energy balances over the network with a Newton iteration, because the pressure-flow system is nonlinear through the friction and component relations.

inputs.name: component-models
inputs.desc: The branch relations that enter the conservation equations

inputs.name: boundary-set
inputs.desc: The boundary conditions that close the system

outputs.name: steady-state-solution
outputs.desc: The converged node pressures and temperatures and branch flows at the operating point

outputs.name: solver-diagnostics
outputs.desc: The residual history, iteration count, and the conditioning or convergence issues encountered

process: Write mass conservation at each node: the sum of branch flows into a node equals the sum out, sum of m_dot = 0, which for incompressible liquid is a volumetric balance. These node equations, together with the branch pressure-flow relations, form the system whose unknowns are node pressures and branch flows.

Write the branch momentum (pressure) relation for each branch: the pressure difference between its nodes equals the component loss plus the elevation term, for example P_i - P_j = f*(L/D)*(rho*V^2/2) + rho*g*(z_j - z_i) for a pipe, with the pump adding a rise and the valve a loss. The nonlinearity in V makes the system nonlinear.

Solve the nonlinear system with Newton-Raphson. Linearize the node and branch equations about the current guess, assemble the Jacobian of residuals with respect to pressures and flows, solve the linear update, and iterate until the mass and pressure residuals fall below tolerance; the classical Hardy Cross loop method is a special case that corrects one loop flow at a time and converges more slowly.

Couple the energy equation for temperatures. Once flows are known, solve node energy balances where each node mixes the enthalpy of incoming streams and each branch adds or removes heat (pipe loss to ambient, heat-exchanger duty); for weak coupling solve flow then temperature, and for strong coupling (temperature-dependent properties) iterate between the flow and energy solves.

Provide a good initial guess and watch conditioning. Seed flows from a simple series-parallel resistance estimate and pressures from the boundaries; a poor guess can send the Newton iteration to a nonphysical negative flow or stall it. Monitor the residual history and the Jacobian conditioning, and add flow limits or relaxation if a branch oscillates between forward and reverse flow near zero.

steps.description: Extend the network model to time-dependent operation and two-phase flow where those matter, adding fluid inertia, wave dynamics, and phase-fraction treatment to the steady network.

inputs.name: steady-state-solution
inputs.desc: The steady operating point used as the initial condition for a transient

inputs.name: component-models
inputs.desc: The component relations extended with inertia and phase behavior

outputs.name: transient-response
outputs.desc: The time history of pressures, flows, and temperatures through the event of interest

outputs.name: two-phase-treatment
outputs.desc: The phase model applied where vapor or cavitation appears, with its range of validity

process: Add fluid inertia for slow transients. The unsteady momentum balance adds the term (rho*L/A)*dQ/dt to each branch, so flows no longer respond instantly to pressure changes; integrate the node and branch equations in time from the steady initial condition to capture pump trips, valve closures, and load changes on the timescale of seconds.

Capture waterhammer for fast transients. A rapid valve closure sends a pressure wave at the acoustic speed a = sqrt(K/rho)/sqrt(1 + (K*D)/(E*t)), where K is the fluid bulk modulus and E and t the pipe wall modulus and thickness; the Joukowsky pressure rise for an instantaneous flow change dV is dP = rho*a*dV, which can be many times the operating pressure and sets burst and support loads. Resolve it with the method of characteristics on a pipe discretized to the wave speed and time step.

Choose the two-phase model by the flow regime. Use a homogeneous equilibrium model (treat the mixture as a single fluid with averaged properties) for well-mixed, near-equilibrium flows; use a drift-flux model where the phases move at different velocities, with the gas superficial velocity j_g = C0*j + Vgj capturing the slip through the distribution parameter C0 and drift velocity Vgj.

Handle cavitation and column separation in liquid transients. When the transient pressure drops to the vapor pressure, vapor cavities form and later collapse, producing severe secondary pressure spikes; include a vapor-cavity model at the affected nodes so the transient does not silently ignore a damaging event.

Match the time step to the fastest physics resolved. Slow inertial transients tolerate large steps, but waterhammer and the method of characteristics tie the time step to the wave speed and pipe segment length (dt = dx/a); verify stability and refine the time step until the peak pressures stop changing, as in any transient convergence check.

steps.description: Validate the network solution against conservation balances and reference points, so the model is accepted on closed energy and pressure accounts rather than on a plausible-looking result.

inputs.name: steady-state-solution
inputs.desc: The steady solution to be checked against balances

inputs.name: transient-response
inputs.desc: The transient result whose peak values and timing are validated

outputs.name: balance-closure
outputs.desc: The mass, energy, and loop-pressure balances with their closure error

outputs.name: validation-record
outputs.desc: The comparison of predicted pressure drops, flows, and temperatures against design data or measurements

process: Close the mass balance at every node and overall. Confirm the sum of flows in equals the sum out at each node to solver tolerance and that total supply equals total demand across the system; a mass imbalance means an unconverged solve or a topology error such as a missing connection.

Close the energy balance across the system. The net heat added (pump work, heat-exchanger duty, pipe losses to ambient) must match the change in fluid enthalpy between inlet and outlet; a persistent energy gap points to a mis-signed heat input, a wrong specific heat, or an unconverged temperature solve.

Check loop pressure balances. Around every closed loop the sum of pressure changes (losses, pump rises, elevation) must be zero; a nonzero loop residual is the direct measure of pressure-solution error and the quantity the network solver drove down, so confirm it is within tolerance.

Compare predicted pressure drops and flows to design points or field data. Check the pump operating point against its curve, the pressure drop across a known valve or heat exchanger against its rating, and branch flows against meter readings; agreement within the instrument and correlation uncertainty (often 5 to 10 percent) validates the component characterization.

Validate the transient peaks and timing. Confirm the predicted waterhammer peak pressure and the arrival time of the wave against the Joukowsky estimate and any measured trace, and confirm the transient settles to the steady solution computed earlier; a transient that does not relax to the correct steady state has an error in the inertia or boundary treatment.

description: Characterize the dynamic behavior of a structure by building the mass and stiffness model, extracting natural frequencies and mode shapes, checking modal mass participation, computing frequency response with identified damping, and correlating the model to test data through the modal assurance criterion.

steps.description: Build the mass and stiffness representation and decide the mass formulation and any degree-of-freedom reduction, because these set the frequencies the eigen-solve will return.

inputs.name: structure-definition
inputs.desc: The geometry, material, connections, and support conditions of the structure

inputs.name: frequency-range-of-interest
inputs.desc: The upper frequency the analysis must cover, set by the excitation it will see

outputs.name: mass-stiffness-model
outputs.desc: The assembled mass and stiffness matrices with the chosen mass formulation and element density

outputs.name: reduction-scheme
outputs.desc: Any degree-of-freedom reduction applied and the frequency range it preserves

process: Set the mesh density from the highest frequency and mode shape of interest, not from a static-stress rule. A mode shape has a spatial wavelength that shrinks at higher frequency; use roughly 6 to 10 elements per half-wavelength of the highest mode you must capture, because a mesh that is fine for stress can be too coarse to represent a high-order mode shape.

Choose the mass formulation. A consistent mass matrix, derived from the same shape functions as the stiffness, is more accurate for a given mesh; a lumped (diagonal) mass matrix is cheaper and preferred for explicit transient runs but tends to under-predict frequencies. Note which you use because it shifts the computed frequencies.

Represent joints and supports with real stiffness. Bolted and welded joints are not rigid; their compliance lowers natural frequencies, and modeling a joint as fully rigid can push a predicted frequency well above the real one. Where a support is flexible, model it as a spring rather than a fixed boundary.

Apply degree-of-freedom reduction when the model is large and only low modes matter. Guyan (static) reduction condenses out the massless or high-frequency degrees of freedom but is accurate only well below the omitted frequencies; component-mode synthesis (for example the Craig-Bampton method) retains a set of fixed-interface modes plus boundary degrees of freedom and preserves accuracy to a stated frequency, which is the method for assembling substructures.

State the valid frequency range of the model. Record the highest frequency the mesh and any reduction can represent reliably (often set at the mesh resolution limit or the reduction cutoff), so later steps do not report modes beyond where the model is trustworthy.

steps.description: Solve the generalized eigenproblem for natural frequencies and mode shapes with a method suited to the model size and the number of modes needed.

inputs.name: mass-stiffness-model
inputs.desc: The mass and stiffness matrices to be solved

inputs.name: reduction-scheme
inputs.desc: Any reduction that sets the effective system size

outputs.name: natural-frequencies
outputs.desc: The extracted natural frequencies up to the range of interest, with any rigid-body modes identified

outputs.name: mode-shapes
outputs.desc: The mass-normalized mode shapes corresponding to each frequency

process: Solve the generalized eigenproblem (K - omega^2*M)*phi = 0, whose eigenvalues omega^2 give the natural frequencies f = omega/(2*pi) and whose eigenvectors phi give the mode shapes. For a single-degree-of-freedom check the basic relation is omega_n = sqrt(k/m), which also gives a quick hand estimate of the fundamental frequency.

Choose the eigensolver by the number of modes and the model size. The Lanczos method is the standard for extracting the lowest tens to hundreds of modes of a large sparse model efficiently; subspace iteration suits a smaller number of modes; avoid dense full-spectrum solvers on large models because cost scales with the cube of the system size.

Extract modes over a range, not a fixed count. Request all modes up to about 1.5 times the highest excitation frequency so the frequency-response and participation steps have the modes they need, including those just above the band that still contribute to the response through their tails.

Identify and handle rigid-body modes. A free or partially constrained structure has up to six zero-frequency rigid-body modes; confirm their count matches the constraint state (a correctly supported structure has none, a free-free model has six), because an unexpected near-zero mode signals a missing constraint or a mechanism in the model.

Mass-normalize the mode shapes so that phi^T*M*phi = 1 for each mode. Mass normalization makes the modal mass unity and the modal stiffness equal to omega^2, which is the convention the frequency-response synthesis and the modal-mass participation calculation assume; mixing normalizations is a common source of wrong response amplitudes.

steps.description: Compute the effective modal mass of each mode and confirm enough modes are retained to represent the dynamic response, using the standard participation threshold.

inputs.name: natural-frequencies
inputs.desc: The extracted frequencies whose participation is assessed

inputs.name: mode-shapes
inputs.desc: The mass-normalized mode shapes used in the participation calculation

outputs.name: modal-mass-table
outputs.desc: The effective modal mass and cumulative participation per direction for each mode

outputs.name: mode-count-decision
outputs.desc: The number of modes needed to reach the participation threshold, with any residual-mass correction

process: Compute the effective modal mass of each mode in each direction. For mode i the effective modal mass is m_eff,i = (phi_i^T*M*r)^2 / (phi_i^T*M*phi_i), where r is the rigid-body influence vector for the direction; with mass-normalized modes the denominator is 1 and the numerator is the squared participation factor. This quantifies how much of the total mass each mode mobilizes in a base excitation.

Sum the effective modal masses and compare to the total mass. The effective modal masses in a direction sum to the total mass of the structure when all modes are included; the cumulative sum as a fraction of total mass tells you how much of the response the retained modes capture in that direction.

Apply the 90 percent participation rule. Retain enough modes that the cumulative effective modal mass reaches at least 90 percent of the total mass in each excited direction, a common seismic and base-excitation requirement; some demanding applications require 95 percent. A direction that falls short needs more modes extracted.

Watch for directions dominated by high-frequency or local modes. A stiff direction may reach the participation threshold only with many modes, or its mass may hide in a local mode; check all three translational and, where relevant, rotational directions, because a design can meet the threshold in one direction and badly miss in another.

Add a residual or missing-mass correction when truncation leaves mass unaccounted. When extracting all needed modes is impractical, add a static correction (a pseudo-mode) that lumps the quasi-static response of the omitted high-frequency modes, so the total response does not lose the stiffness contribution of the modes above the extracted band.

steps.description: Build the frequency response of the structure by modal superposition with a damping model, and identify damping from the response peaks so the predicted amplitudes are physical.

inputs.name: natural-frequencies
inputs.desc: The modal frequencies that locate the response peaks

inputs.name: mode-shapes
inputs.desc: The mode shapes that shape the response between points

outputs.name: frequency-response-functions
outputs.desc: The response per unit excitation across frequency at the points of interest

outputs.name: damping-model
outputs.desc: The identified modal or proportional damping used in the response, with how it was obtained

process: Synthesize the frequency response by modal superposition. The receptance frequency-response function between a response point and an excitation point is H(omega) = sum over modes r of (phi_r*phi_r^T) / (omega_r^2 - omega^2 + 2*i*zeta_r*omega_r*omega), where zeta_r is the modal damping ratio; the sum over the retained modes gives the response, with peaks at the natural frequencies whose height is set by damping.

Choose a damping model matched to the available data. Modal damping assigns a ratio zeta_r to each mode and is the most physical when modal test data exist; Rayleigh (proportional) damping C = alpha*M + beta*K is convenient for direct integration and gives zeta = alpha/(2*omega) + beta*omega/2, but its frequency dependence means it can only match the true damping at two frequencies, so pick alpha and beta to bracket the band of interest.

Identify damping from measured response peaks with the half-power method. For a lightly damped mode the damping ratio is zeta = (f2 - f1)/(2*f_n), where f1 and f2 are the frequencies on either side of the peak where the amplitude falls to 1/sqrt(2) of the peak (the 3 dB points) and f_n is the peak frequency; this reads damping directly off a frequency-response plot.

Use realistic damping values and never zero. Bolted metal structures typically show zeta around 1 to 3 percent, welded structures less, and structures with joints or damping treatments more; a response computed with zero or guessed damping gives infinite or meaningless resonant peaks, so damping is the parameter that most controls the predicted amplitude near resonance.

Check the response against resonance and anti-resonance structure. A correct frequency-response function between two points shows peaks at the natural frequencies and anti-resonances (dips) between them whose pattern depends on the point pair; the presence and location of anti-resonances is a quick check that the mode shapes and their signs are right.

steps.description: Correlate the analytical modes with measured modes using the modal assurance criterion and reconcile differences through model updating, so the model earns the right to predict untested conditions.

inputs.name: mode-shapes
inputs.desc: The analytical mode shapes to be correlated

inputs.name: natural-frequencies
inputs.desc: The analytical frequencies compared against test

outputs.name: correlation-matrix
outputs.desc: The modal assurance criterion matrix pairing analytical and test modes with frequency differences

outputs.name: model-update-actions
outputs.desc: The parameter adjustments that reconcile the model to test, with the physical justification for each

process: Compute the modal assurance criterion between each analytical mode and each test mode. MAC(a, x) = |phi_a^T*phi_x|^2 / ((phi_a^T*phi_a)*(phi_x^T*phi_x)), a number from 0 to 1 that measures the shape consistency between the analytical vector phi_a and the test vector phi_x at the measured degrees of freedom. A MAC above about 0.9 indicates well-correlated mode shapes and below about 0.1 indicates independent shapes.

Read the MAC matrix for pairing and problems. The ideal matrix is near-identity: each analytical mode pairs with one test mode at high MAC and is near zero elsewhere. Off-diagonal high values mean two modes are being confused (often from too few measurement points), and a low diagonal value means a mode shape the model gets wrong.

Compare paired frequencies alongside the MAC. For each well-paired mode report the frequency difference between analysis and test; shapes can correlate well (high MAC) while frequencies differ by several percent, which points to a stiffness or mass error rather than a shape error and tells you what to update.

Update the model against the test with physically meaningful parameters. Adjust uncertain joint stiffnesses, support compliances, or material moduli to bring frequencies and MAC into agreement, changing parameters that are genuinely uncertain rather than tuning arbitrary numbers to force a match; a model matched by non-physical adjustments predicts untested conditions no better than before.

Use operational deflection shapes when a controlled modal test is not possible. Measure the response under operating excitation to obtain the deflection shape at each frequency; unlike mode shapes these include the forcing and damping, so they show how the structure actually moves in service and can reveal a resonance that the forced-excitation test and the model both underweighted.
